statements.quote: Not every query needs the biggest, most expensive model.

statements.quote: A simple "what's the weather?" needs a small, fast model; a multi-step reasoning task needs a large one; a domain question needs a specialized or fine-tuned one.

statements.quote: A router inspects the query and dispatches it — for **cost, quality, and latency** at once — and the common pattern is **cheap-then-escalate**: answer with a small model, and only if it signals low confidence (or the query classifies as hard) do you *escalate* to the big one.

statements.quote: A guardrail is a check that runs **outside** the model, on its input or its output, that the model itself does not enforce.
Input guardrails screen the query (is it in scope?
does it contain PII you are not allowed to process?
is it a prompt-injection attempt?).
Output guardrails screen the answer (does it actually answer the question?
does it contain a prohibited claim or a leaked secret?
does it match the required format?).

The key word is **enforced**: a guardrail is a *layer* the answer must pass, not a line in the system prompt asking the model to "please be careful." A prompt is a *request* to a stochastic component; a guardrail is a *gate* in the deterministic system.

\cite[Rebedea et al., NeMo Guardrails (2023)]{nemocguardrails} is the canonical framing of guardrails as programmable, checkable "rails" the model's output must follow — safety, factuality, format, and scope as *checks*, not *advice*.
This is the same move as the entire course: you do not *trust* the stochastic part to do the thing you need; you *check* it.
Guardrails are the deterministic system's way of holding the model to a contract the model alone would not keep.
When the model can act — read a file, call an API, run a function — the interface is a **schema**: a JSON description of the available tools, their arguments, and their types.
statements.section: The tool-calling schema: a specification the model fills

statements.quote: The model does not "use the tool"; it *fills in the schema* — it emits a structured call (function name + arguments) that the *system* validates and executes.
statements.section: The tool-calling schema: a specification the model fills

statements.quote: This is the [tool use](agents.php) half, but the architectural point is that the schema is a **specification**: a typed contract between a stochastic emitter (the model) and a deterministic executor (your code).
statements.section: The tool-calling schema: a specification the model fills

The reason the first two alone are not enough is the shape of the failures: an LLM product fails **one in two hundred** requests, not one in a thousand.
You cannot debug a failure you cannot *reproduce by name* — the only way to find the 1-in-200 is to have logged the exact prompt that produced the bad answer.
**Observability** is the record of *every call*: the prompt, the completion, tokens in and out, latency, which model it was routed to, which guardrail fired, whether it retried.

\cite[OpenTelemetry GenAI (CNCF)]{otelgenai} standardizes exactly this — the GenAI semantic conventions for tracing LLM calls — so an LLM product has logs, metrics, and *traces* the way any other service does.
It is what makes a probabilistic system *debuggable* at all.
Tools: Langfuse, Helicone, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Honeycomb.
A common production mistake: shipping an LLM endpoint without **cost attribution**.
At scale, a single user can rack up thousands of dollars per session if the system prompt is bloated or the conversation loops.

blocks.section: The reframe: services around a thing that sometimes fails

blocks.quote: The pipeline. A query is routed to the right model, filtered in, answered, filtered out, and checked; if it fails, the retry/fallback loop re-enters the model (dashed) with a different choice; every call is metered. Each box is a service with its own failure mode.
blocks.section: The reframe: services around a thing that sometimes fails

blocks.quote: The router: pick the model per query
blocks.section: The router: pick the model per query

blocks.quote: The cheapest and highest-leverage service is the **router**. Not every query needs the biggest, most expensive model. A simple "what's the weather?" needs a small, fast model; a multi-step reasoning task needs a large one; a domain question needs a specialized or fine-tuned one. A router inspects the query and dispatches it — for **cost, quality, and latency** at once — and the common pattern is **cheap-then-escalate**: answer with a small model, and only if it signals low confidence (or the query classifies as hard) do you *escalate* to the big one. \cite[Ong et al., RouteLLM (2024)]{routellm2024} make this concrete: a lightweight learner, trained on preference data, predicts which model a query needs, and routes the easy ones to the small model — saving the large model's cost on the queries it was never going to beat anyway.
blocks.section: The router: pick the model per query

blocks.quote: Routing is the first place the "the model is a component" reframe pays off: you are not *using* a model, you are *scheduling work across models*, exactly as a system schedules work across machines.
blocks.section: The router: pick the model per query

blocks.quote: Guardrails: enforced layers, not prompts

A guardrail is a check that runs **outside** the model, on its input or its output, that the model itself does not enforce. Input guardrails screen the query (is it in scope? does it contain PII you are not allowed to process? is it a prompt-injection attempt?). Output guardrails screen the answer (does it actually answer the question? does it contain a prohibited claim or a leaked secret? does it match the required format?). The key word is **enforced**: a guardrail is a *layer* the answer must pass, not a line in the system prompt asking the model to "please be careful." A prompt is a *request* to a stochastic component; a guardrail is a *gate* in the deterministic system. \cite[Rebedea et al., NeMo Guardrails (2023)]{nemocguardrails} is the canonical framing of guardrails as programmable, checkable "rails" the model's output must follow — safety, factuality, format, and scope as *checks*, not *advice*.

This is the same move as the entire course: you do not *trust* the stochastic part to do the thing you need; you *check* it. Guardrails are the deterministic system's way of holding the model to a contract the model alone would not keep.
The tool-calling schema: a specification the model fills
blocks.section: The tool-calling schema: a specification the model fills

blocks.quote: When the model can act — read a file, call an API, run a function — the interface is a **schema**: a JSON description of the available tools, their arguments, and their types. The model does not "use the tool"; it *fills in the schema* — it emits a structured call (function name + arguments) that the *system* validates and executes. This is the [tool use](agents.php) half, but the architectural point is that the schema is a **specification**: a typed contract between a stochastic emitter (the model) and a deterministic executor (your code). The executor does not trust the emitted arguments; it *validates* them against the schema, and if the arguments are malformed or out of range, it rejects them and re-prompts. The model proposes; the schema disposes. The [ReAct](react2022) pattern (\cite[Yao et al., 2022]{react2022}) — reason, act, observe, repeat — is the loop this runs in, but the *contract* is the schema, and a schema is exactly the kind of written, checkable standard the [evaluation](evaluation.php) chapter keeps coming back to.
blocks.section: The tool-calling schema: a specification the model fills

blocks.quote: Retry, fallback, and degradation: determinism is built, not had
blocks.section: Retry, fallback, and degradation: determinism is built, not had

blocks.quote: Because the component is non-deterministic, the system must handle its failures *explicitly*, the way a distributed system handles a flaky dependency:
blocks.section: Retry, fallback, and degradation: determinism is built, not had

blocks.quote: The through-line: **determinism is a property you build, not one the model has.** The model gives you a distribution; the pipeline collapses it to a single, checkable, recoverable outcome. The reliability the user experiences is engineered around the model, not supplied by it.
blocks.section: Retry, fallback, and degradation: determinism is built, not had

blocks.quote: > A model is a component. A product is a deterministic system that *schedules* a stochastic component (routing), *checks* it (guardrails), *contracts* with it (schemas), *recovers* from its failures (retry, fallback, degradation), and *sees* and *prices* everything it does (observability, cost). The model is the only box in the diagram you did not design; every other box you did. That is the whole discipline, and it is why "it works in the notebook" and "it works in production" are two different sentences.
blocks.section: Retry, fallback, and degradation: determinism is built, not had

blocks.quote: Observability: The Hidden Half
A production LLM system needs:

The reason the first two alone are not enough is the shape of the failures: an LLM product fails **one in two hundred** requests, not one in a thousand. You cannot debug a failure you cannot *reproduce by name* — the only way to find the 1-in-200 is to have logged the exact prompt that produced the bad answer. **Observability** is the record of *every call*: the prompt, the completion, tokens in and out, latency, which model it was routed to, which guardrail fired, whether it retried. \cite[OpenTelemetry GenAI (CNCF)]{otelgenai} standardizes exactly this — the GenAI semantic conventions for tracing LLM calls — so an LLM product has logs, metrics, and *traces* the way any other service does. It is what makes a probabilistic system *debuggable* at all.
Tools: Langfuse, Helicone, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Honeycomb.

A common production mistake: shipping an LLM endpoint without **cost attribution**. At scale, a single user can rack up thousands of dollars per session if the system prompt is bloated or the conversation loops.

blocks.quote: MLOps / LLM-Ops: life after deployment
Serving is only the start. In production a model is a **system** that drifts, regresses, and costs money:

The discipline borrows its bones from software **continuous delivery** \cite[Wikipedia]{continuous_delivery_wiki} — build, test, ship, observe, repeat — now applied to a model whose "code" is a billion floating-point weights. The goal is the same as in the Evaluation chapter : a measurement loop tight enough that you learn, before a user does, when the model has started to fail.
